Amar Dās, Guru
(A.

—1574)
------------------------------------------
Third in the hierarchy of the Gurus of सिखिस्म्, गुरु Amar Dās has left an indelible impression on the religion and society of the Sikhs during the formative period. Born in A.

as the son of Tej Bhān and Sulakhnī (also known as Lakho or Lachmi) in the village Basarke (near the modern Basarke Gillan in the Amritsar district of Punjab), Amar Dās had practically no formal एदुचतिओन्. Though engaged in trade, the family profession, he had an innate interest in religion which often took him to several places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, especially Hardvār. His strong build enabled him to perform austerities and withstand the rigours of pilgrimages in which he had great faith, imbibed by his deep acquaintance with the Hindu religious traditions. Married to मनसा देवी, he begot two daughters and two sons. Bībī Bhāni, the younger daughter, was later on given in मर्रिअगे to Rām Dās (nicknamed Jeṭha) who succeeded him as the next गुरु.
His quest for inner peace ended when he met गुरु Aṅgad. It was Bībī Amro, a daughter of गुरु Aṅgad that was instrumental in bringing about this meeting. During his long probation of twelve years under the गुरु, Amar Dās had to unlearn many a Hindu custom and deliberately cultivate the Sikh way of life. After he gained गुरु Aṅgad’s confidence, he was directed to return to his family and lead the normal life of a householder.
At the bidding of his गुरु, Amar Dās built the town of Gobindwal, more familiarly called Goindwal, and started living there. It is said that he used to carry the water of the Beas River everyday from Goindwal where he lived, to Khadur where गुरु Aṅgad lived, for the गुरु’s service. This steady and devoted service to the गुरु Aṅgad gained him the गुरु’s grace who finally decided to ordain him as the next गुरु. Amar Dās was nearly 73 years old when the गुरु’s mantle fell on him in A.

. Dātu, the first son of गुरु Aṅgad, who felt he had been deprived of the Guruship that ‘legitimately’ belonged to him, harassed गुरु Amar Dās so much that the latter left Goindwal for an unknown destination. The distressed disciples approached the elderly saint Bhai बुद्ध on whose suggestion, the गुरु’s mare was let free. The mare led them to the गुरु’s hiding place. He was persuaded to return.
Guru Amar Dās trained a number of apostles to spread the message of सिखिस्म्. He is also credited with the performance of several miracles like reviving a dead man, curing a lame devotee as also a mad queen.
The Mughal emperor Akbar is said to have sought audience with the गुरु and was impressed by him very much.
Having had a premonition of the approaching death, गुरु Amar Dās appointed Rām Dās, his son-in-law, as the next गुरु in A.

and shed his mortal coil soon after.
His contribution to the contents of the Guru Granth Sāhib was the third largest. His service to the growth and development of the Sikh community was of a high order.

Amaranātha
(‘Lord of the इम्मोर्तल्स्’)
------------------------------------------
Pilgrimage to holy places is an integral part of the religious observances of the Hindus. Though the number of such places in India is extremely large, only a few have attained great celebrity over the centuries. The अमरनाथ (Śiva) cave in Kashmir is one such. Its importance and antiquity were well-known even by the twelfth century since Kalhaṇa’s Rāja-taraṅgiṇī mentions it.
Situated in the Himalayan ranges at a height of about 4300 metres (13,000 ft.) it lies to the north-east of Srinagar, the capital of Kashmir, at a distance of 138 kms. (86 miles.) It is a big natural cave about 45 metres (150 ft.) in height, 30 metres (100 ft.) wide and 60 metres (200 ft.) in length. Except for a small area, most of the roof leaks. There are two holes in the northern wall of the cave from which water trickles out and freezes into ice almost immediately. One of the holes is bigger and below that a huge लिङ्ग of snow is formed. This is the famous अमरनाथ-लिङ्ग. On its left and right sides there are two more formations of ice, known respectively as गणेश and पार्वती. The cave faces south and the rays of the sun do not fall directly on the लिङ्ग.
There is a traditional belief that the snow लिङ्ग gets formed every lunar month in the bright half and gets dissolved during the dark half. Thus there is no लिङ्ग on the new-मोओन् day and the लिङ्ग attains its maximum size on the full-मोओन् day. Even Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazal (16th cent.) mentions this belief.
Visiting the cave-temple on the Śrāvaṇapūrṇimā day (July—August) is considered extremely auspicious since, according to the mythological lore, शिव appeared in this cave on this day. He made the gods immortal by feeding them with अमृत or nectar. Hence the name Amara-nātha, ‘Lord of the इम्मोर्तल्स्’.
The pilgrims travel in a group from Srinagar. The government makes elaborate arrangements for their comfort and safety.

Amarāvatī
(‘the abode of इम्मोर्तल्स्’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् (Hindu mythological works) delight in describing अमरावती, the capital of इन्द्र’s paradise. Situated on the eastern side of Mt. मेरु it is said to have a thousand gates and a hundred palaces. Full of fragrant flowers and sacred trees and with celestial chariots moving at will, it is the abode of a variety of celestial beings like देवस्, सिद्धस्, apsaras, गन्धर्वस् and others. It can be attained only by those who have performed sacrifices and practised severe penance as also those who die on the battlefield.
There is an अमरावती in Andhra Pradesh, situated on the south bank of the river Kṛṣṇā, about 32 kms. (20 miles) from Guntur. Though a small village now, it was formerly a flourishing city by name Dhānyakaṭaka, the capital of the Śālīvāhana empire (2nd and 3rd cent. A.D.). The Amareśvara temple and the शिवरात्रि celebrations there were famous even by the tenth century A.D. The discovery in A.
of parts of a stūpa by Col. Mackenzie has put अमरावती firmly on the architectural map of India. The great stūpa which took shape between 200 B. C. and A.

and which was bigger than the Sāñcī stūpa must have been 49 metres (162 ft.) in diameter and about 37 metres (120 ft.) in height. The works of sculpture, most of which are in the British Museum, are exquisitely beautiful carvings, mostly in limestone.

Amarakaṇṭaka
(‘peak of the gods’)
------------------------------------------
Places of पिल्ग्रिमगे have exercised enormous influence on the Hindu society. They have contributed not a little, to the preservation of Hindu religion and culture. A river, a mountain, a forest, the seashore or for that matter, any place of natural solitude and beauty—have always attracted the devout and the holy, making them in course of time a regular place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Amarakaṇṭaka hill belonging to the Mekala mountain range in the Bilaspur district of Madhya Pradesh is the place of origin of the famous river नर्मदा. One of the cities of Bāṇāsura destroyed by the arrow of Lord शिव is said to have fallen here. Śrāddha performed here is said to yield great results. It is believed that a person committing religious सुइचिदे here, by ड़स्तिन्ग् or by jumping into fire or water, after purifying himself through certain vows like that of ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy) and अहिṁसा (non-violence), will attain मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्. Even a visit, especially on the days of lunar and solar eclipses, is highly eulogised.
See also NARMADĀ.

āmaśrāddha
(‘śrāddha with raw materials’)
------------------------------------------
It is obligatory on the part of every Hindu to perform śrāddha, a religious rite to please and to benefit the dead ancestors. It is normally performed, with the offerings of cooked ड़ोओद्. However, there are occasions like journey or अशौच (cere-monial impurity caused by the birth of a son and so on) when this will not be possible. The धर्मशास्त्रस् advise that on such occasions आमश्राद्ध can be performed. Other things being the same, uncooked grains take the place of cooked ड़ोओद्, the quantity of the grains being 2 to 4 times the grains required for offering cooked ड़ोओद्. आमश्राद्ध is always prescribed for शूद्रस्.
See also ŚRĀDDHA.

āmalaka
------------------------------------------
These are technical terms used in Hindu temple architecture. The crown of a नागर style of a temple (with curvilinear towers found mostly in North and North-east India) is called आमलक for the simple reason that it resembles an आमलक fruit (myrobalan) in shape. It is a solid ring stone with a cogged rim. It forms the crown of the main शिखर (dome) as also subsidiary śikharas. It clasps the veṇu or the central shaft of the structure. It is not found in the द्राविड temples.
Sometimes, above the usual आमलक, there may be a smaller one of similar shape. In this case, the lower one is called āmalasāra and the upper (smaller) one āmalasārī.
The आमलक is the architectural symbol of the celestial world.

amātya
(‘one who is near’)
------------------------------------------
No civilized life is possible without the protecting hand of a king or a ruler. Among the seven aṅgas or constituents of a State (rājya), the अमात्य (minister) occupies a place next only to that of the king. The other two words that are commonly used to denote a minister are ‘saciva’ and ‘mantrin.’ The ‘saciva’ is a helper or a comrade. The ‘mantrin’ is one who is capable of giving counsel and keeping secrets.
Sometimes the ministers are divided into two groups: dhīsacivas or matisacivas and karmasacivas. The former are also called mantris and are concerned with giving suitable counsel. The latter are responsible for implementing the decisions taken.
Various views are given with regard to the number of ministers in a king’s cabinet. The number usually ranges from 8 to 20 or more.
Though it is obligatory on the part of the king to appoint ministers, it is equally obligatory to test them properly and thoroughly before doing so. कौटिल्य, for instance, lays down (Arthaśāstra 1.10) that the would-be amātyas are to be tested by upadhās (tests of honesty). The tests are designed to make them swerve from the path of their duty (dharma) by tempting them through wealth or woman (artha and काम) or by threats (bhaya), and are conducted secretly.
The ministers, though loyal to the king, were also expected to secure the confidence of the pauras and jānapadas (i.e., the people). This would call for the utmost exercise of tact and courage.
The posts were usually hereditary though the king had the option not to appoint them as ministers if found not suitable.
See also RĀJĀ and RĀJYA.

āmantraṇa
(‘invitation’)
------------------------------------------
Inviting ब्राह्मणस् for partaking the ड़ोओद् during a śrāddha ceremony is an important part of that ritual. The धर्म-śāstras prescribe elaborate rules with regard to the type of ब्राह्मणस् to be invited and also the mode of inviting them.
The two words constantly used in this connection are ‘āmantraṇa’ and ‘nimantraṇa.’ Though they are often used synonymously, subtle distinctions are sometimes made. A ‘nimantraṇa’ is more or less compulsory to accept. If the invitee rejects it without proper grounds, he is said to incur sin. But ‘āmantraṇa’ does not imply compulsion. The invitee has much greater freedom to accept or reject it.

amāvāsyā
(‘living near’)
------------------------------------------
If full-मोओन् has fascinated the ancient man, new-मोओन् must have induced a sort of anxiety and fear. In the Hindu religion, अमावास्या or new-मोओन् has been raised to the status of a deity capable of bestowing wealth and valiant sons on the supplicant (vide Atharvaveda 7.79[84].2).
On this day the मोओन् is not visible from the earth. She is believed to be with the sun (amā = near, vāsyā = living), and is seen only by the sun. Hence the other name ‘darśa’ for अमावास्या.
Two kinds of amāvāsyās are recognised: सिनीवाली when it is mixed with caturdaśī tithi (the 14th day after fullmoon) and कुहू when mixed with pratipad (the 1st day after new-मोओन्). Even these are sometimes referred to as deities who can be supplicated.
One of the well-known वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, the Darśa, has to be compulsorily performed on this day.
Amāvāsyā falling on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday is considered as especially holy. So also, if it is associated with the nakṣatras as अनूराधा, Viśākhā or Svātī. Several vratas (religious observances) are recommended to be performed on such days.

Amarakoṣa
(‘immortal lexicon’ or ‘Lexicon of अमरसिṁह’)
------------------------------------------
Lexicography is one of the important branches of technical literature in Sans-krit. The Nighaṇṭu, a vocabulary of Vedic words, is the oldest lexicon so far known. The Nirukta of यास्क (800 B. C.) is a commentary on it.
But among the extant lexicons of Sanskrit, the Amarakoṣa (also spelt as Amarakośa) of अमरसिṁह (A.

), a Buddhist scholar, who might have adorned the court of विक्रमादित्य, is the best known and the most widely used.
Popularly known as the Nāma-liṅgānuśāsanam (‘a work which deals with vocables and their genders’), it is divided into three ‘kāṇḍas’ or books or sections. (Hence the name Trikāṇḍa also.) The first called Svargakāṇḍa deals with heavenly matters. The second called Bhūmikāṇḍa deals with earthly things. The third called Sāmānyakāṇḍa is concerned with general matters.
The whole work is in poetry, in the anuṣṭubh metre. The major part of the work deals with synonyms and only a small section called Nānārthavarga is devoted to homonyms.
Being the most popular of such lexicons, the Amarakoṣa has sixty commentaries. Out of them the Amarakoṣod-ghāṭana by क्षीरस्वामिन् (11th cent A. D.) seems to be the earliest. Ṭīkāsarvasva of Sarvānanda (12th cent. A. D.) is a more scholarly work.
